deep_why: This work learns useful graph features by comparing multiple corrupted views of the same graph and rewarding consistency across levels. The core computation measures similarity between node pairs across different graph damage patterns. Why this works: when two views are corrupted differently but drawn from the same underlying structure, nodes that remain close in all views must carry real semantic signal rather than noise specific to one corruption. The method applies this by building loss functions at three scales simultaneously—individual nodes, clusters, and the whole graph—so early learning layers learn node facts while deeper layers learn how facts compose into structure. This three-scale consistency guarantee forces the model to discover features robust enough to predict both fine and coarse patterns.

The core problem is compressing a user's thousands of past actions into a short sequence for modern recommendation models while keeping two conflicting things: actions stay coherent within each segment and gaps between segments stay small. Traditional compression either groups actions uniformly or by similarity, but both destroy one property while preserving the other. This approach solves it by building segments that respect both constraints at once—items cluster together AND stay temporally close—so the compressed representation faithfully maps back to the original timeline. This dual guarantee works because items close in time and similar in meaning share causal roots in user intent, so treating them as one unit loses less information than treating them separately.

The core problem is estimating available network capacity from imperfect signals. Video encoding produces frames of wildly different sizes—a high-motion scene suddenly explodes in bytes—so sending at a fixed rate either wastes capacity or causes packet loss. The solution measures capacity not at the packet level where encoding jitter dominates, but at the frame level where the data is naturally grouped. Why this works: frames are the true units of information delivery; a frame is either sent or not, buffered or not, with consequences visible to the viewer. By measuring how long frames take to traverse the network in aggregate rather than counting tiny packet timings, the algorithm extracts the true bottleneck speed, immune to encoding's internal choppiness. This frame-level view directly mirrors how video actually flows and stalls, so bandwidth estimates stay accurate even when encoding is irregular.

The core challenge is combining signals from many different types of user behavior data—login records, file access, email metadata—each in different format, each with signal but also noise. Naive ensemble voting fails because a strong signal (like normal file patterns) drowns out a weaker but rare threat signal (like access at 3 AM). This method solves it by mapping all signals into a common hidden space where it can learn which ones point toward actual threats, then reweighting each signal's contribution based on what the data reveals. Why this works: threats leave traces across multiple channels, but not equally in each one; a coordinated analysis that learns which channels matter most for each type of threat, and how to balance them, recovers threat patterns that single-view methods miss. The geometric alignment into one space ensures all signals inform the same hidden threat representation.

The core idea is treating large language model conversations like crime scenes: capturing interaction history as tamper-resistant records, replaying the model's decisions under the same input conditions to verify they repeat, and detecting when manipulated prompts trick the model into breaking safety rules. Why this works: if a model produces different outputs on identical inputs, something in its state changed—a sign of adversarial manipulation. By capturing not just final answers but the sequence of prompts and response identifiers, and replaying those sequences in isolation, investigators can isolate which prompt caused a safety violation and reproduce it under control. This replay-and-diagnosis method is sound because model behavior is deterministic once you fix the input and initial state, so discrepancies between original and replayed runs reveal exactly where the model went wrong.

Finding images related to a reference photo plus a text description requires reasoning across two different types of information. The core computation is scoring which database images match both the visual intent and textual edits of the query. Why this works: the method delegates each type of reasoning to a specialist agent—one imagines what the text modifications should create visually, one finds visual similarities, one verifies semantic consistency—then coordinates them iteratively. This works because each agent builds on the previous one's candidates; early agents cast a wide net, later ones narrow with semantic verification. The guarantee is that by forcing agents to reason in sequence and check each other's work, false positives that satisfy one criterion but not another get filtered, leading to results that satisfy both image and text intent simultaneously.

The core problem is answering questions whose answers are not written down anywhere but must be deduced from hints scattered across multiple documents. Retrieving one perfect document does not solve it because no single document contains the answer. The method's soundness rests on a key insight: when a question needs inference, the supporting passages provided by the retriever contain clues that together triangulate the answer. By treating retrieval and reasoning as separated processes that each measure different things—first finding passages with high clue density, then reasoning across multiple clues to derive what they imply—the system can succeed where extractive methods fail. This separation works because it respects the structure of inference itself: assembling pieces of evidence then synthesizing them into a conclusion neither piece alone supports.

The core problem is knowing when a search agent has found enough information to answer versus when it needs to search more. Current agents optimize for final answer quality, not search quality, so they learn to search excessively. The solution identifies misaligned decision boundaries—the hidden threshold in the agent's mind for when to stop—by comparing search trajectories where the decision changed. Why this works: if an agent decides to stop searching at one point but would have decided to continue with slightly different information, that decision point is poorly calibrated. By collecting examples of decision boundaries from causal reasoning about what-if scenarios, and retraining the agent to align boundaries with true sufficiency rather than superficial optimization, the agent learns when accumulated knowledge truly answers the question. This is sound because search decisions become cost-benefit judgments: stop when benefit of one more search is less than its cost.

Finding groups of nodes in networks where edges are labeled positive or negative is hard because conflicting signals—positive edges within a group, negative edges between groups—can be noisy or contradictory. This method refines detected communities by iteratively fixing inconsistencies. The core computation adjusts node membership to reduce internal edge conflicts and boundary confusion. Why this works: communities are stable structures where positive edges reinforce membership and negative edges point outward; noise causes misclassifications. By comparing each node's edge patterns to the current community assignment and moving nodes to groups where they fit better, the algorithm pushes toward a state where communities minimize internal conflict. This iterative tightening is sound because each move reduces conflict energy, driving the solution toward a locally consistent structure where the signal dominates noise.

The core problem is training models on data from many different wearable devices and users, where each source has its own data distribution that the model has never seen. The solution generates new synthetic training examples designed to cover unseen distributions. Why this works: real data from different users and devices differs in subtle ways—signal strength, timing patterns, frequency content—making the model overfit to seen sources. By learning the frequency patterns—the speed of oscillations and peaks—that characterize each source, then mixing frequency patterns in new ways the training data never combined, the method creates synthetic examples that teach the model robustness. This is sound because frequency patterns are low-level statistical signatures independent of raw pixel or value scales; mixing them teaches the model invariance. The generalization works because it forces the model to learn which frequency patterns predict class labels rather than memorizing source-specific quirks.

Foundation models trained on general image and text data encode shared features useful for many tasks, but item embeddings from these models treat all users the same—they don't account for different users caring about different item aspects. The solution assigns different tuning modules to user groups so each module learns to highlight aspects relevant to that group's purchases. Why this works: a shoe image has many observable aspects—color, comfort, brand, price—and different users attend to different ones. By conditioning the embedding transformation on inferred user group, each group's module learns to enhance its group's predictive aspects. This is sound because it respects that meaning is use-dependent: the same image feature serves different predictive purposes for different users, so grouping lets each module specialize. The guarantee is mathematical: with separate modules per group, features can be transformed independently for each, capturing group-specific attention patterns that monolithic models cannot.

The core problem is that gig platforms can exploit worker uncertainty about labor costs by posting low prices, knowing most workers will accept because they underestimate their true effort cost. The mathematical model shows the platform pays only a logarithmic fraction of true labor value by exploiting high uncertainty. The reason this works: workers don't know their costs precisely, so the platform bets that most will misjudge themselves as willing to work cheaper than they actually are. However, if even a small coalition of workers commits to a price floor and coordinates, they become reliable enforcers: the platform must pay them fairly or lose them entirely. The soundness is in the economics: when some supply is inelastic to price (the coalition won't budge), the equilibrium price shifts dramatically. The platform can no longer exploit mass uncertainty because a strategic minority breaks the exploit, forcing all workers' reservation prices upward.

Misinformation often contains multiple intents layered together—some claims aim to inflame emotions, others spread false facts, others promote a group. Understanding which intents are present improves detection. The method learns a set of concept axes that represent pure intents, then scores each claim by how much it expresses each intent. Why this works: intents are directions in a meaning space; each claim combines them in different proportions. By learning these axes from data without labels, then using a mixture model to explain each claim as a blend of intents, the method separates signal. This is sound because real claims are indeed blends: a piece of misinformation might be 30 percent emotionally inflammatory and 70 percent factually false. Modeling claims this way lets the detection system reason about which intents predict veracity, capturing that some intents are more reliable truth-markers than others.

Transferring knowledge from one network to a different one requires finding node representations that work across domain shift. The core computation is learning features that stay useful even when network structure and node types differ between source and target. Why this works: rather than building complex, handcrafted architectures, this method uses a simple propagation-transformation pipeline—neighbors influence each other, then features are updated—applied at different depths. Having two copies of this pipeline with different depths lets the model learn both local and global structure from the same data. The method leverages multiple source networks simultaneously by pooling their learned features, then matching target distribution to this pool. This is sound because simpler pipelines are less prone to overfitting to source-specific quirks, so they transfer better. Having both shallow and deep versions ensures no information is lost: some nodes need local context, others need graph-scale structure.

Psychological support requires not just answering but guiding a person through stages of therapy—first helping them understand their problem, then building insight into its roots, then practicing new behaviors. The method orchestrates multiple agents to follow this clinical structure. The core computation balances staying in the current stage appropriately while advancing progress. Why this works: therapy is staged because early stages create foundations for later ones; rushing to action before the person understands their problem causes backsliding. By having specialized agents for each stage plus routing logic that chooses which therapeutic school fits the client's needs, the system enforces clinical soundness. A recording agent continuously converts free conversation into structured clinical notes, making the process accountable and replayable. This is sound because it grounds the system in established therapeutic practice: exploration builds case understanding, insight reframes the problem, action implements change—following this sequence matches how human therapy succeeds.
